source_read: Only BRIEF.md, tasks_reader421.json and the four original supplied PDFs were used. Kandel (1975), Science 190, pp. 912–914; Wagner and Anthony (2002), Am J Epidemiol 155, pp. 918–925; Lynskey et al. (2003), JAMA 289, pp. 427–433; Morral et al. (2002), Addiction 97, pp. 1493–1504. Independently extracted source text and rendered all 30 PDF pages at 150 dpi in /workspace/scratch/d1ee8d93ce58/tmp/pdfs/reader421_20261110; inspected relevant page images and own 300 dpi table/figure renders, including Kandel Table 2, Wagner Table 2, Lynskey sample figure and Tables 2–3, and Morral Figures 3–4. Reproduced the labelled conversions and correlation-squared calculations independently. No other reader outputs, project claims, study cards, adjudication logs, editor notes, live browsing or downloads were used.

results.note: The two percentages and the printed N≥342 and N≥467 labels are correct at p. 913. The denominator for 27% is more specific than having ever used all three legal-drug classes: Table 2 and the preceding text classify exclusive legal-drug users by current use in the past 30 days at the initial survey. The replacement makes that baseline scope explicit and restricts the absence of inferential reporting to these Table 2 estimates. Note 4 describes wave weights for school/homeroom selection probabilities and school response, followed by reweighting of the high-school panel to reproduce the baseline marijuana-use frequency in the complete cross-sectional sample; these are survey/panel weights, not covariate adjustment.
results.corrected_extracted: Between fall 1971 and spring 1972, cannabis (marihuana or hashish) use was reported by 27% of the New York State high-school panel group who were exclusive legal-drug users and were currently using cigarettes, hard liquor and beer/wine at the fall survey (past 30 days; Table 2 labels total N≥342), compared with 2% of those who had never used any drug at that survey (total N≥467). These are survey-weighted percentages; no statistical tests, uncertainty intervals or covariate-adjusted estimates accompany these Table 2 percentages. Note 4 describes weights for school/homeroom selection probabilities and school response, plus high-school-panel reweighting after linkage loss to reproduce the time-1 marijuana-use frequency in the complete cross-sectional sample.

results.note: The crucial-step/stage wording is indeed in both the abstract and the running text, including two statements in the p. 913 left-column paragraph beginning Sequences of change. The p. 914 body contains the non-invariable progression, stopping/regression and probable cultural-determination caveats. The dependence of the number of stages on drug classification is specifically in note 3, not the running-text caveat paragraph. The replacement preserves the supported within-body tension while attributing that classification caveat precisely.
results.corrected_extracted: The paper uses crucial-step language for cannabis in the abstract (p. 912) and crucial-step/crucial-stage language in the running text (p. 913), not only in the abstract. The body also says that a particular drug does not invariably lead to drugs higher in the sequence, that many youths stop or regress, and that the stages are probably culturally determined (p. 914). Note 3 adds that the specific number of stages varies with the classification of drug behaviors used in an analysis. Thus the strong crucial-step/stage language and the caveat about non-invariable progression both occur within the body of the paper (editorial reading), alongside the separate classification caveat in the notes.

results.note: Methods pp. 919–920 support the four 1991–1994 surveys, 1994a subsample, response-rate range 79.2%–85.3%, 44,624 cocaine-analysis participants aged 12–25, integer recalled ages, person-year data, time-varying drug events, demographic covariates and additional age at first marijuana use in cocaine models. The four printed cocaine sample sizes sum independently to 44,624. Risk sets are defined jointly by census tract/city block group at assessment and survey year. Conduct problems and family/peer drug use do not appear in the described adjustment set; that reporting limitation does not establish that the wider surveys failed to measure them. The cited location is adequate.

The source reports 136 monozygotic and 175 same-sex dizygotic discordant pairs at p. 428 (independent sum 311). Statistical Analyses, p. 429, explicitly pools zygosity and sex after interaction tests with P>.10. Tables 2–3 print pooled estimates, with no principal before-17 monozygotic-only estimates. Subsidiary Analyses, p. 431, reports separate zygosity analyses using before-15, before-16 and before-18 cutoffs and says they confirmed the conclusions without printing estimates. The stated psychiatric and early-use covariates are described on p. 429; tables identify the significant covariates retained for each outcome. Peer affiliation and temperament are not described as measured covariates in this article, which is not proof of nonmeasurement in the registry. The shared-family-background control follows from the pair comparison; residual genetic differences in dizygotic pairs are a sound editorial limitation, not a reported estimate. Nonsignificant zygosity interactions do not establish equivalence of monozygotic and dizygotic effects.

The p. 1499 survey calculation is explicitly hard-drug use by 21 among respondents aged at least 22, stratified by whether marijuana had been used by 21; it does not impose marijuana-before-hard-drug ordering. Hard drugs are defined at pp. 1497–1498 as heroin, cocaine or hallucinogens. The model-output description spanning pp. 1499–1500 uses prior-marijuana-initiation wording, so the extraction correctly treats comparability of the two estimands as unsettled rather than declaring that they differ. Reported 157 and 24, ordering proportions 0.011 and 0.016, and the same-year-order limitation are printed on p. 1500; p. 1501 also prints 11 and 16 per 1,000. Independent calculations give 0.011×1,000=11 and 0.016×1,000=16. Own 300 dpi Figure 3 confirms rising hazard ratios over frequency under all four assumed correlations (0, 0.4, 0.8, 1). No uncertainty intervals accompany these reported results. A source notation inconsistency remains: p. 1500 prints YH<YM for an initiation-order criterion although earlier Y denotes opportunity ages and Z initiation ages; the explicit narrative supports the extraction, but that printed inequality should not be used to resolve the definition independently.

The indicator construction at p. 1501 controls its correlation with true propensity through normally distributed error variances. Own 300 dpi Figure 4 on p. 1502 confirms printed odds-ratio labels 297, 178, 82, 32, 12, 2 and 1 at the stated positions; approximately 0.95 for the 12 label is an appropriately qualified reading of its plotted x-coordinate rather than a printed numeric x-value. The text itself calls 0.99 a correlation and associates it with about 2% uncaptured propensity variance, despite using reliability on the axis and in nearby prose. Independently, 0.8²=0.64 (64% in the stated simple linear interpretation), and 1−0.99²=0.0199 (1.99% uncaptured), so correlation and variance have been distinguished correctly. The passage concerns odds of hard-drug initiation by age 22, with marijuana-use status as predictor, rather than a causal cannabis effect.
